title: Normal-subgroup ind-unipotence of discrete profinite representations
statement: Let $G$ be a profinite group (a compact Hausdorff totally disconnected topological group), let $H\triangleleft G$ be a closed normal subgroup, and let $R$ be a commutative ring. A discrete continuous $R$-linear $G$-module means an $R$-module with a $G$-action by linear automorphisms for which each element has open stabilizer. Call such a module $H$-unipotent if it admits a finite filtration by $G$-stable $R$-submodules with trivial $H$-action on every successive quotient, and $H$-ind-unipotent if it is a filtered colimit of $H$-unipotent discrete continuous $G$-modules. Then the $H$-ind-unipotent modules are closed under submodules, quotient modules, extensions inside the category of discrete continuous $G$-modules, and all small colimits; the inclusion preserves their kernels and cokernels. Equivalently, writing $I_H=\ker(R[H]\to R)$ for the augmentation ideal of the group algebra (the map sends $\sum_h a_h[h]$ to $\sum_h a_h$), $M$ is $H$-ind-unipotent if and only if every $m\in M$ is annihilated by $I_H^q$ for some integer $q\geq0$. If $M$ is finitely generated over $R$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], this is equivalent to $H$-unipotence, or to $I_H^qM=0$ for some single $q$. The zero module is included. No Noetherian hypothesis on $R$ is imposed, and the middle term in the extension assertion is required to have a discrete continuous action.

source.place: Expose XVII, Definitions 11.1.1-11.1.2, Proposition 11.2.1(ii),(iii),(vii),(ix)-(xi) and Propositions 11.3.1-11.3.4, pp. 327-330. The profinite hypothesis is used for extension closure.

proof.text: Write $I=I_H$. Every augmentation-zero sum is $\sum_h a_h([h]-1)$, so $I^q$ is spanned over $R$ by words $([h_1]-1)\cdots([h_q]-1)$; the empty word for $q=0$ is $1$. Put $F_qM=\{m:I^qm=0\}$. These are increasing $R[H]$-submodules with $F_0M=0$. Conjugating a word by $g\in G$ replaces its letters by $g^{-1}h_ig\in H$. Thus $F_qM$ is $G$-stable. Also $I F_{q+1}M\subset F_qM$, so $H$ acts trivially on $F_{q+1}M/F_qM$.

source.place: XVII 11.1.2, 11.2.1(vi), and opening paragraph of 11.3, pp. 328-330

proof.text: A filtration $0=M_0\subset\cdots\subset M_q=M$ with $H$-trivial quotients satisfies $IM_i\subset M_{i-1}$; iteration gives $I^qM=0$. Conversely, if $I^qM=0$, Step 1 gives $0=F_0M\subset\cdots\subset F_qM=M$ with $H$-trivial quotients. Submodules inherit open stabilizers; a quotient has open stabilizers since any representative's stabilizer fixes its class. Thus these are filtrations in the discrete continuous category. This proves unipotence equivalent to a uniform augmentation-power bound, including $q=0$ for $M=0$.

Call $M$ locally annihilated when each element is killed by some $I^q$. Submodules preserve this condition by restriction, and quotient modules preserve it by lifting an element. Arbitrary direct sums preserve it because each element has finite support: the maximum of its finitely many component exponents kills it. Direct sums remain discrete continuous, since a finite intersection of open stabilizers fixes each finite-support element; quotients remain so because a representative's stabilizer fixes its class.

For a small diagram $(M_i)$, form $D=\bigoplus_i M_i$ and quotient by the $R$-span $K$ of $\iota_jf(x)-\iota_i x$ for all arrows $f:i\to j$. Equivariance gives $g(\iota_jf(x)-\iota_i x)=\iota_jf(gx)-\iota_i(gx)$, so $K$ is $G$-stable. An equivariant linear map out of $D$ kills $K$ exactly when its component maps commute with all arrows. Thus $D/K$ has the colimit universal property in the discrete continuous category. Step 3 ensures discreteness and local annihilation of $D/K$ if these hold for the $M_i$; the empty diagram gives zero.

Steps 2 and 4 imply that every filtered colimit of unipotent modules is locally annihilated. Conversely, for locally annihilated $M$, the increasing $G$-stable submodules $F_qM$ of Step 1 exhaust $M$, and Step 2 makes each $F_qM$ unipotent. Their inclusions form a filtered diagram indexed by $\mathbb N$. Compatible equivariant linear maps on its terms extend uniquely to $M$ by evaluating an element in any term containing it; passing to a larger term proves independence. Thus $M$ is their filtered colimit. This proves the asserted equivalence; Steps 3-4 give submodule, quotient and small-colimit closure.

For $M$ finitely generated over $R$ as in [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_t$. If $M$ is locally annihilated, choose exponents $q_i$ killing these generators and take $q=\max_i q_i$, with $q=0$ for $t=0$. Then $I^q$ kills each generator and all their $R$-linear combinations, since the action is $R$-linear. Thus $I^qM=0$; the converse is immediate. Step 2 identifies this with unipotence. No assertion about finite generation of $R$-submodules is used.

source.place: XVII 11.2.1(ix), p. 329, for finite generation over R

proof.text: Fix an ambient short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\xrightarrow{\pi}C\to0$ with locally annihilated endpoints, and $b\in B$. By [lem-exc-discrete-continuous-action-finite-orbit-coproduct], the underlying discrete continuous $G$-set is covered by finite invariant subsets. One containing $b$ contains $Gb$, so $S=Gb$ is finite. Let $N=\mathbb Z S\subset B$ be the additive subgroup generated by $S$. It is $G$-stable, and its action factors through the finite permutation image $P\subset\operatorname{Sym}(S)$, since $S$ generates $N$. Write $Q\subset P$ for the image of $H$. Choose an exponent $a$ killing every $\pi(s)$, $s\in S$, using the maximum of finitely many exponents in $C$. For $J=\ker(\mathbb Z[H]\to\mathbb Z)$, the word description of Step 1 gives $J^aN\subset\ker\pi=A$.

source.place: XVII 11.2.1(ii), proof p. 329, and 11.3.4; finite-orbit reduction

proof.text: For the objects of Step 7, $J^aN$ is the abelian subgroup generated by the finite list $T=\{(u_1-1)\cdots(u_a-1)s:u_i\in Q,\ s\in S\}$. To check this equality, expand every factor of an augmentation-zero integral sum into integral multiples of $[h]-1$, and write elements of $N$ as integral combinations of $s\in S$; their actions depend only on the images $u\in Q$. Conversely, lift each $u_i$ to $H$ to see that every listed word belongs to $J^aN$. For $a=0$ the list is $S$.

source.place: XVII 11.2.1(ii), proof p. 329, and 11.3.4; explicit finite-word argument replacing the integral Noetherian-subgroup argument

proof.text: By Step 7, every $t\in T$ belongs to $A$, hence is killed by some augmentation power. Take the maximum $c$ of these finitely many exponents (zero if $T$ is empty). Integral words of length $c$ kill every generator in $T$, hence all their integral combinations, giving $J^c(J^aN)=0$. In particular $J^{a+c}b=0$. Step 1 identifies integral and $R$-coefficient annihilation on a vector: both mean that every word of that length kills it. Thus $I_H^{a+c}b=0$ in $B$. Since $b$ was arbitrary, Step 5 proves extension closure. No Noetherian hypothesis on $R$ was used.

source.place: XVII 11.2.1(ii), proof p. 329, and 11.3.4; explicit finite-word argument replacing the integral Noetherian-subgroup argument

proof.text: For an equivariant linear map $f:M\to N$ between ind-unipotent modules, the ordinary kernel is $G$-stable and inherits open stabilizers, while $N/f(M)$ has open stabilizers by lifting representatives. The usual module universal factorizations are equivariant: use the kernel's injective inclusion and the cokernel's surjective quotient. Thus these are the ambient categorical kernel and cokernel. Submodule and quotient closure from Steps 3 and 5 put them in the ind-unipotent full subcategory, where the same universal properties apply. Its inclusion therefore preserves both. The zero module is killed by $I^0=R[H]$, and is included throughout.

proof_origin.place: XVII 11.1-11.3, pp. 327-330; expands colimits and replaces the integral Noetherian-subgroup argument with an explicit finite word list.

The H-action factors through the finite permutation image, so J^aN is generated by the finite word list T, and J^{a+c}b=0, then I^{a+c}b=0. This correctly replaces the source's 'N de type fini sur Z' Noetherian step.
